s: (1919–2009) was an American organizational theorist, one of the founders of operations research, and one of the most quotable voices in systems thinking. He trained as an architect, earned a PhD in the philosophy of science at the University of Pennsylvania, and taught at Case Institute of Technology and later Wharton for decades. He also consulted for hundreds of organizations, Anheuser-Busch most famously.
In his November 1993 talk at the
conference, Ackoff argued that we're in the early stage of a shift as big as the Renaissance. We're moving from the
, which understands things by taking them apart, to the
, which understands things by seeing the larger whole they belong to.
Big idea 2 · A system is more than its parts

A system's essential properties belong to the whole, not to any part. No single part of a car can carry you across town, and if you take a car apart you no longer have a car, even if you keep every piece. As Ackoff put it in many talks, a system is not the sum of its parts but the product of their interactions.
Big idea 3 · Organizations are social systems
Managers often run companies as if they were
(bodies that just want to survive and grow). Ackoff argued that a company is a
: it has purposes of its own, its people have purposes of their own, and it sits inside a society with its own purposes. Treat it like a machine and it pushes back.
Big idea 4 · Leadership is an aesthetic act
Ackoff held that leadership is poorly understood because it is mainly an
function. A leader does two aesthetic things:
offering a vision so attractive, so
, that people want to pursue it.
making the pursuit itself satisfying and fun, so people find it worth doing for its own sake.
Inspiration without implementation is provocation, not leadership. Implementation without inspiration is management or administration, not leadership.
Ackoff's distinction, as quoted in later writing on his leadership paper.

If Ackoff is right, most "fixes" fail because they improve parts instead of the whole. Most leaders also fail because they manage means without inspiring ends. "The righter we do the wrong thing," he liked to say, "the wronger we become."
From Mechanistic to Social Systemic Thinking
. A condensed version was published in

as "From Mechanistic to Social Systemic Thinking" (Ackoff, with Kellie Wardman). What follows is a guided, section-by-section study of the talk's argument in my own words. To read the article itself, see the
The arc in one line: our
came from the Renaissance and built the Machine Age. Its assumptions have broken down, and a new Systems Age needs a different way of thinking:
Ackoff opens by saying that each of us carries a theory of reality, a

, that we absorbed growing up and rarely examine. Worldviews change only rarely, and we're living through one of those changes right now. He compares its scale to the move from the Middle Ages into the Renaissance.
what is one belief about how organizations "work" that you absorbed without ever choosing it?
2. How the Renaissance built the Machine Age worldview

Ackoff sketches the Middle Ages: short lives, high infant mortality, most people never travelling far from where they were born, and attention fixed on the afterlife. Contact between cultures, through the Crusades and the trade of the Italian city-states, reawakened interest in
world. Out of that came three beliefs that defined the modern mind:
In principle we can understand everything. He recounts the 19th-century confidence that science would wrap up the universe within a few decades.
To understand something, take it apart down to indivisible elements, explain the parts, then assemble those explanations into an explanation of the whole.
All relationships are cause and effect.
Ackoff draws out three consequences of treating everything as cause and effect:
Following causes back leads to a first, uncaused cause, which the era identified with God.
If the cause alone is sufficient, nothing else matters, so you can study a cause and its effect in isolation, as in a laboratory.
Everything that happens was made to happen by something earlier. There's no room for chance or choice.

Newton's universe was the perfect expression: a closed, self-running mechanical clock. Ackoff then lays out a three-step argument that he says launched the Industrial Revolution. The universe is a machine created by God. Man is made in God's image. So man should create machines.
4. The Industrial Revolution and the Machine Age
Work came to mean applying energy to matter to transform it. Industrialization

work by breaking it into the simplest possible tasks, which could then be done by machines or by people acting like machines. Frederick Taylor's task decomposition is the emblem. The factory became a network of elementary tasks, and the cost was the
where in your own work are people asked to behave like interchangeable parts?
5. The dilemmas that cracked the Machine Age
if everything is determined, choice is an illusion. Thinkers couldn't live with that.
Heisenberg's uncertainty principle showed that some things can't be known completely, even in principle. Ackoff cites John Dewey's view that understanding is an ideal we approach but never reach.
in the mid-20th century, Norbert Wiener's cybernetics and Ludwig von Bertalanffy's general systems theory offered a different way of thinking about wholes.
6. The Systems Age: what a system is

is a whole made of two or more parts, where each part can affect the behavior of the whole, and none has an independent effect, because each part's effect depends on what the others are doing. The crucial consequence:
A system's essential properties are properties of the whole. No part has them, and when you take the system apart it loses them.

a car's essential property is carrying people from place to place. A wheel can't do that, nor an axle, nor a carburetor. Disassemble the car, keep every part, and you no longer have a car. So analysis, which takes things apart, can never reveal what makes a system a system.
7. Analysis vs synthesis; knowledge vs understanding
Analysis is still useful: it reveals
a system works the way it does. That's
Identify a larger system that contains the thing you want to understand.
Explain the behavior of that containing whole.
Explain the thing by its role or function within the whole.

analysis tells a mechanic how a car works. Synthesis explains why American cars were designed to seat six: the car was a family vehicle, and the American family averaged about 5.6 people when those designs were set. As family size fell, cars shrank. You only see that by looking
to the family and society, not inward at the engine.
to understand your team, don't start with its org chart. Start with the organization it serves, ask what that organization is trying to do, then ask what your team's role in it is.
The Systems Age swaps the Machine Age doctrines for new ones:
replaces reductionism. Understanding grows by expanding the system you look at. Complete understanding is never reached, but larger wholes give deeper understanding.
complements cause–effect. Ackoff credits his teacher E. A. Singer Jr. for the idea. A producer is
for its product. An acorn is necessary for an oak, but throw it into the ocean or onto an iceberg and you get no tree. It also needs soil, water and light. So explanation becomes
: you can't explain anything without its environment.
become compatible with scientific explanation. Cause–effect and producer–product are complementary views of the same world. Ackoff compares this to cutting an orange in different directions.
9. Business: machine, organism, or social system?
Ackoff traces how the business enterprise was conceived:
: the owner's instrument, with no purpose of its own
The owner was effectively the "god" of the firm. Workers, often barely surviving, did what they were told.
: survival and growth are its purposes
Growth needed more capital than owners could reinvest, so ownership spread to shareholders and professional managers took over.
: the whole, its parts and its environment all have purposes
A better-educated workforce with safety nets was no longer driven only by survival. Movements for civil rights, women's liberation and youth showed the "parts" asserting their own purposes.
The trouble, Ackoff says, is that most managers still run social systems with machine or organism thinking.
10. The technology of the Systems Age
The Machine Age's signature technology was
, machines that replace muscle by applying energy to matter. The Systems Age's signature is
. Ackoff traces the line from measuring instruments, through the telegraph, telephone, radio and television, to the electronic computer.

Our problems now arise in a world of social systems, yet we keep attacking them with mechanistic or organismic thinking. Until that mismatch is fixed, Ackoff warns, quality of life, and perhaps even standard of living, will keep eroding.
Ackoff's most surprising claim about leadership appears in "A Systemic View of Transformational Leadership" (
, 1998) and related writing. He says leadership has been poorly understood largely because it is
. To see why, you need his map of what people pursue.
Following the ancient Greeks, Ackoff names the ideals humans pursue. The Greeks identified three, and modern society added a fourth. Each has its own institution or field:
Peace, cooperation, the absence of conflict
Ackoff observed that organizations invest heavily in the first three: R&D, finance, compliance. Yet they barely think about the fourth, which is exactly where leadership lives.
Creation: beauty that pulls you forward
side of aesthetics is the sense of getting somewhere, of developing toward something worth having. A beautiful vision or ideal
: it makes people willing to give effort and to accept short-term sacrifice. This is why ideals matter even though they can never be fully reached. Their job is to pull.
side is the satisfaction we get from an activity itself, regardless of its outcome: play, fun, flow. Recreation
us. It refreshes mind and body and restores energy for the long pursuit. Ackoff argued that work should carry this satisfaction too, which is why he cared so much about the quality of work life.
A leader is the person who supplies both: an
(recreation). That's why Ackoff can call leadership an art. Like an artist, the leader works with "materials," here people, purposes and organizations, to produce something others find compelling.
Inspiration without implementation is provocation, not leadership. Implementation without inspiration is management or administration, not leadership.
directs others toward ends using means that someone else selected. A
directs others and selects the means, and perhaps the ends. A
. The key difference is voluntariness. You can order compliance, but you can only
commitment, and inspiration is an aesthetic act.
(increasing one's ability and desire to satisfy one's own needs and those of others). A transformational leader cares more about development. In his account, such a leader:
Formulates, or facilitates the formulation of, an inspiring vision.
Ideally it's co-created, so followers see their own purposes in it.
Finds ways and means of pursuing it
, turning the vision into action and keeping it moving.
others to pursue the vision voluntarily, and makes the pursuit enjoyable.
This links straight back to the 1993 talk. In a
the parts are people with their own purposes. You can't make a social system work by command, as you would a machine. You have to align purposes, and that's what an inspiring, shared ideal does.
In later writing Ackoff argued that leadership is an
that requires talent. Like other arts it can be
. A course can teach you about the materials and tools, as an art school teaches about paint, but not how to make something others find beautiful. That comes from practice, reflection and feedback.
An aesthetic audit of your own leadership
Use these questions on the plane. Score each from 1 to 5.
could everyone on my team state where we're going in a sentence, and would they find it
, worth effort for its own sake?
did they help shape it, or did they receive it?
do people enjoy the work itself? When did someone last describe a week as fun?
if I stopped checking, would the work still get done because people want it done?
are my people becoming more able, or are we just getting bigger?
If your scores are low on creation and recreation but high on execution, Ackoff would say you're managing, not leading.
The ideas Ackoff returned to across his career, all following from systems thinking.
: whether the whole and its parts have purposes of their own.
No: your heart has no purpose of its own
A company, a university, a city
The mistake Ackoff saw everywhere is managing a social system as if it were a machine (people as parts) or an organism (only survival and growth matter).
Ackoff argued that managers don't face independent problems. They face dynamic situations of interacting problems, which he called
. Solving each problem separately usually makes the mess worse, because the problems interact. Manage the mess as a whole.
Four ways to treat a problem
Ignore it and hope it goes away
Do something "good enough," based on experience and common sense
Find the best possible answer, often through research and models
Redesign the system so the problem can no longer arise
Dissolving is Ackoff's favorite. The best way to handle a recurring problem is often to change the system that produces it.
Ackoff's signature method. Assume the system you're responsible for was
, but its environment is untouched. What would you build in its place
, if you could have anything that's technologically feasible and operationally viable? Design that ideal, then work backward to get as close as possible.

Ackoff traced the idea to a 1951 story about Bell Labs. A leader told researchers to assume the telephone system had been destroyed and to design the one they'd want instead. Innovations such as push-button phones are said to have followed. Idealized design is aesthetic leadership in practice. It creates a beautiful, shared ideal, and designing it together is energizing.
(predict the future and prepare for it), and
(design a desirable future and invent ways to bring it about). Interactive planning has the people affected take part in designing it. Participation matters more than the plan.
In 1989 Ackoff described a hierarchy that's now often drawn as the "DIKW pyramid":
: data processed to answer who, what, where, when, how many.
: answers how, the know-how that makes information usable.
: evaluated understanding, judging what's worth doing, the effectiveness that values bring.
His jab was that education and management pour effort into the bottom layers and almost none into understanding and wisdom.
is how well you use resources to reach an objective; it's value-free.
is efficiency weighted by the value of the objective. Doing the wrong thing efficiently is worse than doing the right thing badly, because you get further in the wrong direction.
The righter we do the wrong thing, the wronger we become.

In many lectures Ackoff told a story about building the best car by taking the best engine, the best transmission, the best brakes and so on from different manufacturers. You wouldn't get the best car. You wouldn't even get a car, because the parts don't fit together. Improving each part separately doesn't improve the whole, and can make it worse. What matters is how the parts interact.

Five exercises that turn Ackoff's ideas into practice. Each takes 10–20 minutes with a notebook. A seat-back tray works fine.
your team or job is part of.
by its role in that whole
. Does today's work match that role?
Assume your team (or product, or process) vanished last night. Its customers, market and constraints remain. On one page, design the version you'd build
, limited only by feasibility, not by the past. Then circle the three gaps between that design and reality that would matter most.

List the 5–8 problems currently stressing you. Draw arrows wherever solving one would make another better or worse. Look for the problem with the most arrows: that's your leverage point. Then ask whether any of them could be
by a redesign instead of solved.
Score your team from 1 to 5 on
(is there an inspiring, shared vision?) and on

(is the work satisfying in itself?). For each, write one concrete thing you could do in the next two weeks to raise it by a point. Examples: co-write a one-sentence ideal with the team; kill a soul-draining recurring process; celebrate progress toward the vision, not just output.

Find one place where your organization treats people as interchangeable parts: a rule, a metric, a process. Ask what purpose those people bring to the work, and how the design could serve their purposes as well as the organization's.
Ackoff's test for any change: does it make the
better, by improving how the parts interact, or does it just make one part look better?

glossary.d: 1919–2009. American organizational theorist, operations-research pioneer and systems thinker; taught at Case Institute of Technology and the Wharton School.
The worldview from the Renaissance through the mid-20th century: everything can be understood completely, by analysis, as chains of cause and effect.
The emerging worldview Ackoff described: understanding comes from wholes and their environments, through synthesis and expansionism.
The usually unexamined theory of reality a person or culture holds.
A whole of two or more parts, each able to affect the whole, none with an independent effect. Its essential properties belong to the whole and are lost when it's taken apart.
Taking a thing apart to explain its parts. Reveals structure: how it works. Produces knowledge.
Explaining a thing by its role in the larger system that contains it. Reveals function: why it works as it does. Produces understanding.
The Machine Age belief that everything can be explained by reducing it to ultimate, indivisible elements.
The Systems Age doctrine that understanding grows by expanding the system considered, though complete understanding is never reached.
A relationship in which the cause is both necessary and sufficient for the effect. Implies determinism and environment-free explanation.
A relationship in which the producer is necessary but not sufficient for the product (an acorn and an oak). Requires the environment and leaves room for choice.
Whether an explanation ignores the surroundings (lab-style) or must include them.
The belief that everything that happens was made to happen by prior causes, leaving no room for chance or choice.
Using machines to replace human muscle: applying energy to matter. The key technology of the Machine Age.
Using machines to replace human mind: observing, communicating and manipulating symbols. The key technology of the Systems Age.
A system with no purpose of its own; it serves its user (a car).
A system with purposes of its own (survival, growth) whose parts have none (a body).
A system with purposes of its own whose parts also have purposes, inside a larger system with purposes (a company).
Ackoff's term for a system of interacting problems; what managers actually face.
Four ways of treating a problem: ignore it; do something good enough; find the best answer; redesign the system so it can't arise.
Designing the system you'd create right now if the current one had been destroyed last night, then closing the gap.
Designing a desirable future and inventing ways to bring it about, with the people affected taking part.
Truth (science), plenty (economics), the good (ethics) and beauty (aesthetics).
The pursuit of beauty. For Ackoff it has two faces: creation (inspiration) and recreation (enjoyment).
The inspiring pull of an ideal; the sense of getting somewhere worth going.
The satisfaction of an activity for its own sake; it refreshes and re-creates energy.
Leadership that brings about development, not just growth, through an inspiring vision pursued voluntarily.
Growth is getting bigger or having more; development is increasing one's ability and desire to satisfy one's own and others' needs.
Efficiency: how well resources achieve an objective (value-free). Effectiveness: efficiency weighted by the objective's value.
Data, information, knowledge, understanding, wisdom: Ackoff's 1989 hierarchy of what minds contain.
Philosopher at the University of Pennsylvania who taught Ackoff; source of the producer–product idea.
Annual conference run by Pegasus Communications; Ackoff spoke there in November 1993.

qs: When and where did Ackoff give "From Mechanistic to Social Systemic Thinking"?
November 1993, Systems Thinking in Action conference
November 1993, at the Systems Thinking in Action conference organized by Pegasus Communications.
What two ages did Ackoff say we are moving between?
From the Machine Age (analysis, cause-effect) to the Systems Age (synthesis, wholes).
If you take a car apart and keep every piece, you have…
A system’s essential property, moving people, belongs to the whole and is lost when it’s disassembled.
A system is best described as…
The product of its parts’ interactions
Ackoff: a system is not the sum of its parts but the product of their interactions.
Ackoff said leadership is primarily what kind of function?
He argued leadership is poorly understood because it is primarily aesthetic: inspiring (creation) and satisfying (recreation).
"The righter we do the wrong thing…"
Efficiency in pursuit of the wrong objective only takes you further from where you should be.
What did Ackoff train in before operations research?
He earned an architecture degree, then a PhD in philosophy of science at Penn.

decks.name: The Talk
qs: Which was NOT one of the three Renaissance beliefs Ackoff describes?
All relationships are cause and effect
Synthesis is the Systems Age alternative. The Renaissance trio was complete understandability, analysis, and cause-effect.
In cause–effect thinking, a cause is…
That’s why explanation became environment-free: if the cause is sufficient, nothing else matters.
Analysis gives knowledge of how something works; synthesis gives understanding of why.
The first step of synthesis is to…
Identify a larger system that contains it
1) find the containing whole, 2) explain the whole, 3) explain the part by its role in the whole.
Why did American cars seat six?
The average family was about 5.6 people
Synthesis: the car’s role in the family explains its design. As families shrank, cars did too.
An acorn thrown into the ocean makes no oak. It needs an environment, so explanation is environment-full.
The key technology of the Systems Age is…
Mechanization replaced muscle; automation replaces mind by observing, communicating and manipulating symbols.
Which thinkers did Ackoff credit with the systems break in the mid-20th century?
Norbert Wiener (cybernetics) and Ludwig von Bertalanffy (general systems theory).
Ackoff’s closing warning was that we…
Attack social-system problems with mechanistic or organismic thinking
The mismatch between our problems and our thinking erodes quality of life.

decks.name: Leadership
qs: Ackoff’s four ideals are truth, plenty, the good and…
Beauty, pursued through aesthetics. The Greeks had truth, good and beauty; modern society added plenty.
The two faces of aesthetics are…
Creation: the inspiring pull of an ideal. Recreation: enjoyment of the activity itself.
And implementation without inspiration is management or administration, not leadership.
What most distinguishes a leader from a manager in Ackoff’s view?
A leader induces others to follow voluntarily; you can order compliance but only inspire commitment.
Development, increasing ability and desire to meet needs, matters more than growth (getting bigger).
Can leadership be taught, according to Ackoff?
It’s an art: it can be developed, not simply taught
Like an artist, a leader can learn about materials and tools, but the art comes from talent, practice and reflection.
Recreation helps a team mainly by…
Restoring energy, re-creating people for the long pursuit
Enjoyment of the work itself refreshes people and sustains effort toward a distant ideal.
